title: Advanced Memory Optimization
description: Reduce Redis memory footprint with encoding selection, key expiration, and data-structure-aware design.

data.text: Redis stores everything in memory, so every byte matters. A poorly designed cache can consume gigabytes of RAM for data that would fit in megabytes with smarter encoding. Memory optimization is not just about saving money — it directly affects how much data you can keep hot, how quickly Redis responds, and whether your instance survives traffic spikes without evicting critical keys.

Redis uses two internal encodings for hashes: ziplist and hashtable. When a hash has fewer than a configurable number of entries and each value is small, Redis stores it as a ziplist — a compact, contiguous memory block. Once the hash crosses the threshold, Redis converts it to a hashtable with better read performance but higher overhead. You can control these thresholds with hash-max-ziplist-entries and hash-max-ziplist-value.

data.text: Many Redis memory problems come from using the wrong data structure. Storing JSON as a single string prevents Redis from understanding your data. A hash lets you access individual fields, use ziplist encoding, and expire specific fields if needed. Similarly, using a sorted set when you only need uniqueness wastes memory; a set is the correct choice.

Memory Command
data.text: Run MEMORY USAGE <key> to see exactly how much RAM a key consumes. Run MEMORY DOCTOR to get optimization suggestions. Run INFO memory for a full breakdown of Redis memory usage by component.

Redis supports per-key expiration with EXPIRE and TTL. For large-scale caches, use LRU eviction (maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru) so Redis automatically evicts the least recently used keys when memory is full. This is far better than allowing Redis to run out of memory and crash, or manually managing eviction in your application code.

items: Use hashes instead of JSON strings for related fields
Set EXPIRE on every key to prevent unbounded growth
Monitor MEMORY USAGE for keys larger than expected
Choose allkeys-lru or volatile-lru eviction policy
Avoid storing large blobs when smaller chunks suffice

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use hashes instead of JSON strings to enable ziplist encoding
Set TTL on every cache key to prevent memory leaks
Configure LRU eviction to protect Redis from OOM
Use MEMORY USAGE and INFO memory to audit usage
data.takeaway: Memory optimization starts with data-structure choice. A hash that fits in ziplist encoding can use 90% less memory than the same data stored as a JSON string.
